The systemic formula

1Explore a dungeon branch
2Finish an enemy with the exact number
3Collect a monster part or plant
4Cook a Dish Card at a campfire
5Spend a portion in the next battle

This is the strongest concept in the set because combat, loot, and deckbuilding do not exist separately. Precise Cut turns lethal-damage arithmetic into an economic decision: an exact kill produces a cooking resource. At a campfire, up to two ingredients become a dish, a short timing check affects its quality, and the result is a Dish Card with limited portions. Eating a card can heal, block, attack, or apply an effect, and the resource disappears when its portions run out.

Controls observed in the recording. Movement and interaction use point-and-click controls on corridors and highlighted objects; M opens the map. In combat, the player selects a card with the mouse, aims it at a target, and then confirms End Turn. Hovering opens tooltips.

How the first session unfolds

00:00–01:19

itch.io page → developer note → menu → settings → Randy selection → starter pack → loading.

01:45–03:09

The Vending Machine supplies a starter kit; onboarding introduces movement, the map, item pickup, and the choice to eat now or carry a resource.

03:09–05:11

First turn-based fight: energy, target selection, enemy intent, block, and Precise Cut. The reward connects victory to parts and cards.

05:21–06:46

Midnight Service → gold → campfire → ingredient selection → timing minigame → creation of a Dish Card.

06:54–08:01

A chest opens Partchinko, then the Singing Mushroom Choir grants a card; the complete Deck is opened.

08:16–10:36

A three-enemy fight demonstrates target selection, enemy intents, poison, and consumable dishes.

10:36–11:50

Your Haul → new or upgraded card → relic → Merchant with buying, removal, and upgrades → the next resource object.

Combat: clear parts, complicated sum

The base combat language is familiar for a deckbuilder: hand at the bottom, card costs, 3/3 action points, End Turn, HP bars, block, and enemy intents. A card is held and directed at a target, with predicted damage visible in advance. Precise Cut adds exact arithmetic, while dishes introduce consumable effects.

By the second fight, the player is reading three targets, poison, status tooltips, temporary defence, and new cards at once. Every element is individually explainable, but onboarding arrives as a sequence of modal prompts while the player is already parsing the board.

Observed resources

  • HP and Hunger
  • 3 action points per turn
  • Gold
  • Parts / ingredients
  • Dish Card portions
  • Regular cards and relics
  • Starter choice and future characters

Exploration: many events, a distant run goal

The map makes the floor structure visible, but in 11:50 the player encounters a Vending Machine, map, combat screen, Midnight Service, cooking, Partchinko, Mushroom Choir, Deck, reward haul, and Merchant. The run feels rich, yet the broader question—how far remains to the main test of the run?—is answered less clearly than each local prompt.

What works

Every resource has an origin

A dish is not a random card after battle. The player created it from earned material, giving the effect a history.

Exact lethal damage becomes mastery

Precise Cut forces the player to recalculate a familiar attack. It changes card choice without adding a separate combat subsystem.

Rooms change the pace

Combat is not followed by the same reward screen every time: a service, cooking, a physics minigame, an event, and a shop alternate decision types.

Visual cohesion

Cards, characters, weapons, and food belong to one illustrated world. Even interface minigames feel like parts of the dungeon.

What slows understanding

A long route to the unique formula

The “kill → part → cook → use dish” chain takes roughly six minutes to unfold. Before that, the game resembles a conventional dungeon deckbuilder.

Many modal lessons

The prompts explain mechanics but fragment the pace and compete with small card and status tooltips. Reset Tutorials in accessibility settings acknowledges their weight.

Weak run hierarchy

It is locally clear what to click, but less clear which boss or milestone the route leads towards and why a specific choice advances that objective.

A mixed public signal

Product depth does not change the fact that visible reach currently validates the development story more strongly than the game itself.

Transfer

Connect combat mastery to the economy of the next phase. Precise Cut matters because it creates a new decision, not merely a bonus number.

Avoid

Do not open ten interfaces before the player has repeated the central loop twice. Depth should unlock at the pace of mastery.

Experiment

Show Precise Cut → Part → Dish → Portion as a four-step track. Measure Precise Cut success, first cooking completion, and dish use in the second battle.

Reason to return

Potentially, a new route and recipe produced by the previous fight. Return is not measured in this recording because it does not reach death, a boss, or a second run.

Screen-by-screen product anatomy

Interface specification

A reconstruction-oriented inventory of the visible hierarchy, controls, states, interruptions, and feedback in Cook the Dungeon. It describes observed recording evidence first; recommendations are explicitly labelled.

Evidence convention. Observed means the state is visible in the reviewed session or captured UI. Implementation guidance marks a production requirement inferred from the interaction model, not a claim about unseen code.

Viewport map

Exploration canvas

A first-person corridor fills the center; interactable vending machines, doors, ingredients, and event objects receive spatial outlines/prompts rather than permanent large labels.

Combat workspace

Enemy intent and health occupy the upper playfield; the player hand forms a bottom rail; AP, HP, block, statuses, and End Turn frame the tactical decision.

Run-management layer

Map, deck, campfire cooking, merchant, event, haul, settings, and character/starter selection use modal sheets that pause or clearly gate movement.

Overlays & interruptions

  • Route map and deck browser, each with a clear close key and paused movement.
  • Card/keyword tooltips anchored to hovered or focused UI without covering costs and targets.
  • Campfire ingredient sheet, timing challenge, and dish result as three explicit phases.
  • Merchant, Partchinko, Mushroom Choir, haul summary, and relic reward panels.

Motion, VFX & feedback

  • Card hover lift, targeting line, impact flash, floating damage/block/heal, and status tick sequencing.
  • Exact-lethal Precise Cut gets a unique target cue and ingredient reward burst.
  • Corridor interactables gain proximity outline; pickups fly or count toward the inventory HUD.
  • Cooking meter uses a moving marker and colored accuracy zones; result presentation distinguishes portions and quality.
  • Room/event transitions dim or freeze the 3D view so panel input never leaks into movement.

Responsive, accessibility & edge cases

  • Every card and status must have keyboard-focusable tooltip access; hover cannot be the only explanation path.
  • Offer a reduced camera-bob/flash option and scalable card text for first-person accessibility.
  • On smaller screens, show one enlarged selected card and a scrollable hand rather than illegibly shrinking the full row.
  • Persist run state at room boundaries and before/after merchant or cooking commitments; prevent duplicate purchase resolution.
Reconstruction test. A player should be able to identify a room interaction, open and read the route map, predict an enemy turn, play and resolve a card—including an exact-lethal ingredient harvest—cook a dish, buy/remove an item, and verify every inventory or currency change.
03
Creator context · verified public sources

Developer dossier

Who made Cook the Dungeon, the public context around the work, and the nearest verified projects. Private identity, location, employment, and credits are left unknown unless the creator or an official project page states them.

Public identity and credit

Danny Limanseta is credited as developer and publisher on the official Cook the Dungeon pages. His public profile describes him as a product designer and co-founder at Nurture and Reroll; the broader game-making effort is also presented under the Vibeforge name.

Location and working context

No specific public location was verified—the profile’s “Earth” label is intentionally non-specific. Professionally, Limanseta describes a product-design and startup background rather than a conventional long-term game-studio résumé.

Timeline

He says he began experimenting with AI-assisted or “vibe-coded” development in early 2025. The Cook the Dungeon browser demo was published on 18 August 2026 as a work in progress ending after Pantry Depths / Act 1; its Steam release is currently planned for 2027.

Other verified work

The official itch profile also lists Banners Will Fall, described as a dark-fantasy auto-battler roguelike. A broader Patreon/Vibeforge page describes collaboration with game-industry veteran Aldric Chang on making a full game for Steam, but Cook’s store credit remains Danny Limanseta as developer/publisher.

Visible development pattern

The work combines product-design framing, rapid AI-assisted implementation, public browser validation, and a planned commercial PC path. Cook the Dungeon is built as a systems-dense vertical slice: first-person navigation, deck combat, ingredient harvesting, cooking skill checks, events, and merchants.

What this means for the teardown

Separate the verified surface from implementation speculation. The recording proves a coherent Act 1 stack, while later acts, final content volume, and Steam production values remain future scope. AI-assisted workflow does not by itself establish which assets or subsystems used which tools.

Identity boundary. Professional and collaboration claims here come from the creator’s public profiles. No more precise residence, team composition, or asset authorship is inferred beyond explicit credits.

04
Reconstruction blueprint

What must exist to rebuild the observed game

This is a product and systems specification derived from the public build and the recorded first session. It describes observable behaviour, not the original source-code architecture.

Reconstruction confidence. High for the recorded onboarding through the second fight and merchant. Medium for recipe quality, the full route structure, bosses, characters, and run-to-run progression.

State machineSession flow

  • Character / starter selection → load a run with HP, Hunger, deck, and initial resources.
  • Node exploration → move through a first-person corridor map and interact with encounters.
  • Turn combat → spend three action points on cards, inspect enemy intent, then end the turn.
  • Exact kill check → Precise Cut rewards a monster part only when lethal damage matches remaining HP.
  • Campfire cooking → select up to two ingredients, complete a timing check, and mint a consumable Dish Card.
  • Reward / service / event / shop → alter deck, relics, gold, ingredients, or health before the next branch.

Input contractControls

  • Point-and-click movement and interaction in corridors and highlighted room objects.
  • M opens the route map; mouse hover opens card, status, and object tooltips.
  • In combat, click a card, aim it at a target where required, resolve it, and press End Turn.
  • Cooking uses ingredient selection followed by a separate timing-meter interaction.

Rules engineSimulation and resolution

  • The player begins a turn with three action points; cards consume points and can attack, block, heal, or apply status.
  • Enemy intent forecasts upcoming actions; block is temporary unless an effect says otherwise.
  • Precise Cut is an exact-arithmetic condition, not a generic overkill bonus.
  • Ingredients are earned objects; cooking combines up to two and produces a Dish Card whose quality depends on timing.
  • Dish Cards live in the combat deck but have limited portions and disappear when consumed.
  • HP, Hunger, gold, parts, normal cards, dishes, relics, and route position create overlapping resource clocks.

Meta layerEconomy and progression

  • The Vending Machine establishes the starter kit and first consumable decision.
  • Combat rewards lead to parts and cards; campfires convert parts into authored consumables.
  • Events such as Midnight Service, Partchinko, and Mushroom Choir vary reward interaction rather than repeating one panel.
  • The Merchant sells cards and relics and offers card removal and upgrades, enabling deck compression as well as growth.
  • Character and starter choices imply run archetypes, but their full differentiation was outside the session.

Required screen and interface inventory

Menu, settings, accessibility, and tutorial reset
Character and starter-pack selection
First-person corridor and interactable node
Branching map with encounter legend
Turn-based combat with hand, AP, HP, block, statuses, and intents
Combat reward / Your Haul
Campfire ingredient selection and timing minigame
Dish Card result with portions
Partchinko and scripted service/event panels
Deck inspection
Merchant purchase, removal, and upgrade interface

Minimum useful data model

  • CardDefinition: cost, target type, damage/block/heal payload, status operations, tags, upgrade branch, exhaust/portion behaviour.
  • EnemyDefinition: HP, intent deck, status resistances, ingredient drop table, exact-cut part reward.
  • IngredientDefinition and RecipeRule: tags, pair outcome, timing-quality thresholds, resulting dish and portions.
  • RunState: character, HP, Hunger, gold, deck, relics, pantry, map seed, current node, visited events.
  • EncounterDefinition: 3D room presentation, interaction script, reward table, next-node transitions.

06
Production sequence

Build the causal loop before the content surface

A practical implementation order for reproducing the observed promise while keeping the prototype testable at every step.

  1. Prototype turn combat with AP, intents, block, three enemies, and exact lethal detection.
  2. Connect exact kills to parts, then parts to one campfire recipe and a limited-portion Dish Card.
  3. Add a small node graph with combat, campfire, event, reward, and merchant so the entire loop repeats twice.
  4. Expand cards, statuses, ingredients, recipes, relics, characters, and room scripts as data-driven registries.
  5. Finish onboarding with a persistent four-step tracker: Precise Cut → Part → Dish → Portion used.

Boundaries and unresolved behaviour

Do not encode these as facts yet.
  • The recording does not reach a boss, death, full run reset, or meta-progression screen.
  • The exact formula connecting timing accuracy, ingredient pairs, dish quality, and portions remains partially observed.
  • Hunger depletion, character-specific systems, seasonal-card rules, and complete relic interactions need additional sessions.

What this document is built from

Radar data explains discovery and public traction. The local recording, transcript, on-screen tutorial text, and marker frames explain the observable product. Neither layer proves unobserved source code or late-game behaviour.
